Hi Jo,

Could you let me know when the shelf brackets are expected? We hope to open our shared craft cupboard on Tuesday, provided they arrive by Monday afternoon.

The cupboard is beside the north window. Blue labels mark tools, which only workshop members can borrow. White labels mark paper, which anyone attending an open session may use in the room. Both are free.

Thanks for helping us get this ready!

Mina

Hi Eli,

Thanks for offering to bring the folding chairs. We need six for Saturday; if you can bring only four, that is fine too. Please leave them inside the side entrance.

Best,
Ruth

I tried a borrowed shallow tray for the stamp pads at two club sessions. They were easier to find, which was encouraging, although we had fewer people than usual. I suspect the tray helped; I cannot quite separate its contribution from that of a quieter room. Apparently a place to put things counts as an innovation. Before buying trays for every group, I would try it again with a full table and see whether the idea survived the company.
I prefer a small trial before we buy more trays. The first session looked promising, but the room was unusually quiet. That is an observation, not yet a result.

Green cards reserve workshop places; orange cards put people on the waiting list. Both need a name and contact number. Collect them at the afternoon’s end, after packing away boxes and sample materials. Collection does not turn orange cards into reservations: their holders need a cancellation and the organizer’s confirmation by phone to get a place. Green-card holders need no extra call.

After the afternoon session, you may take lantern kits home, including the smaller sample lantern. Leave the large demonstration kit on the long table. Return kits to the grey basket by noon the following Friday. If you cannot meet that deadline, tell Noor before taking a kit home.

I would support another limited trial to investigate the questions June left unanswered. Log A recorded 14, 9, and 16 visits between 6 and 7 p.m. across three Thursdays, but returning visitors could be counted twice; unique visitor numbers are unknown. Memo B says the experiment ran only in June, when two local classes were running. We do not know whether those classes influenced attendance. The proposed three-week October trial has not been approved (Memo B). If it goes ahead, counting unique visitors and asking about class attendance would help address these gaps before deciding whether to continue late opening.
The desk recorded eight exchanges on the first Saturday and eleven on the second. Rain on the first day may be relevant, but these notes do not tell us whether it affected attendance.

In the town of Buttonmere, Ada set her painted biscuit tin lid beside the shoebox theatre. Her uncle Basil inspected it with the gravity he usually reserved for damp sandwiches.

“A shield,” he said. “Excellent. Who's invading?”

“It's the moon.”

Basil turned it over. “Rather substantial for a moon.”

“It had biscuits in it yesterday. It's adjusting.”

A chip at the edge showed bare metal through the silver paint. Basil offered to cover it with a star, but Ada said the moon had been through enough without repairs. She threaded a string through a hole near its rim while he arranged three paper trees on the tiny stage.

The tallest tree fell across the curtain.

“Wind,” Basil said promptly.

Ada raised the chipped moon above the shoebox. Basil leaned close to examine the effect, sneezed, and sent the entire forest into the orchestra pit.

Ada handed him the tweezers.

I fetched a chair and sat facing the box, as though it had arrived for an audition. There was a faint scrape when I nudged it away from the mountain. I couldn't tell whether something inside had shifted or the painted cardboard had caught beneath it.

Under Leo's note, in smaller writing, I noticed: Keep it upright.

That was useful advice to discover late. I straightened the box and checked its single lock again. It stayed shut. I wondered what I would say to Vera on Sunday, beginning with how to introduce myself.
